body: Following your feedback, I required at least 5 percent minority-group approval. I started with 0.005 times B and used the predeclared descending sequence only if needed. The common selected value is 0.0003125. Group B reaches at least 5 percent approval and remains below Group A in both risk scenarios. The models remain frozen from the previous run. They learned from 80,000 training applicants, and all lending and profit results use the separate 20,000 prediction applicants. I frame the comparison as naïve OLS estimation, direct discrimination through an added penalty, and a more flexible gradient-boosting estimator, without assuming that ML must win.

body: This makes the split explicit. The training subset mimics past loan information and prior noisy risk measurements. OLS and Gradient Boosting use permitted characteristics and the credit proxy to learn PN. The bank does not observe true PD or every determinant of risk. We then apply frozen models to a separate prediction subset, add the manual group penalty only in that branch, clip scores for economic accounting, and select a common cutoff under capital. We calculate profits only from those prediction applicants. For ML, its original 64,000/16,000 fitting-validation subdivision is entirely within the 80,000 training applicants, followed by an 80,000-row refit. No model was refit for this 5% approval-floor update.

body: In the first risk scenario, Group A and minority Group B are generated under the same underlying risk conditions. This does not require their finite sample means to be numerically identical. Neither the OLS control nor Gradient Boosting includes B. The bank with direct discrimination adds a positive penalty after estimation, despite the lack of an underlying group treatment in true risk. This lets us compare an unadjusted estimate with the same estimate plus arbitrary discriminatory treatment.

body: These are three methods under Scenario 1, not three different applicant populations. OLS control is the naïve linear risk estimator. The discriminatory method uses exactly the same fitted OLS score and adds 0.0003125 times B. Gradient Boosting is the flexible predictive comparator, with performance evaluated empirically rather than assumed to be superior. The information set is Y, D, C; B is excluded from the first scenario fitted models. The common penalty was selected using prediction-cohort approval rates to reach at least 5 percent in both scenarios while remaining below Group A. This does not contaminate the model-fitting split with prediction labels, but the policy choice is not an untouched confirmatory evaluation.

body: All results here use the same 20,000 prediction applicants, never the 80,000 training applicants. For Scenario 1, the selected common penalty is 0.0003125 times B, added to the frozen OLS raw score before clipping. Group A has 3450 approvals out of 16970 and minority Group B has 383 out of 3030. Group B therefore reaches the inclusive 5 percent minimum and has a lower approval rate than A. The true expected portfolio profit difference from control is −$23.3K. The profit bars sum each group's funded-loan contributions, so unequal group sizes matter. ML uses 72.4065 percent of capital; its next indivisible prediction block cannot fit under the common cutoff. More approvals need not mean greater capital use or greater profit. These are nominal synthetic expected values, not annual realized returns.

body: The second scenario represents a systemic difference outside this bank’s lending decision, potentially analogous to unequal treatment in other domains or the past. We do not claim real-world evidence about why any actual group is riskier. The existing synthetic world shifts epsilon by one standard deviation for Group B and updates C consistently. The noisy measurement uses the same eta. That existing risk response is modest because the frozen sigmoid is near saturation. We preserve it without retuning. Both fitted methods include B in this scenario. Changing both risk conditions and the feature set means the cross-scenario contrast is not a pure epsilon-only causal effect.
